subtype: Approach: arguing on and on with no decision [Pitfall]
passage: The Class 5 art period was forty minutes, and the group of four spent all of it arguing. "Our title should be 'Green Earth'!" said Francis. "No, 'Save Water'!" said Sachin. Then came the colours: blue, green, blue and green again. Neither would give way, and the other two watched the clock. When the bell rang, the chart paper on the desk was still blank, with only a pencil line across it. The teacher stopped at their table. "The chart is due on Friday," the teacher said, looking at the empty sheet. Francis and Sachin looked away, and nobody spoke on the way out.

qa.q: When is the chart due?
qa.a: The chart is due on Friday.

qa.q: What might Francis and Sachin be feeling when the teacher points at the empty sheet?
qa.a: Francis and Sachin are probably embarrassed and worried, shown by looking away and going out without speaking. 😰

qa.q: What alternative approach could the group try, and why might it help?
qa.a: They could set a short time to decide and toss a coin if they cannot agree. A limit turns endless talk into a decision so work can begin.

qa.q: How might the other two group members see the argument?
qa.a: The two who watched the clock were probably frustrated and anxious, since the argument used the whole period and put their shared chart at risk.

grounding: The group argues about the title and colours for the whole period, so nothing is made and the deadline is close.

subtype: Approach: setting a time limit for deciding [Action]
passage: I'm Indu. Last week our group could not choose a topic for our project, and we had been going in circles since Monday. Ishita said the sports day would be good, and Nikhil wanted space. I looked at the clock and had an idea. "Let's give ourselves five minutes. If we can't decide by then, we toss a coin." Everybody agreed, and Nikhil set the timer on his watch. We each said our reasons quickly. Sports won by two votes, and we did not even need the coin. We started drawing before the bell rang, and I felt relieved. It was simple, but it worked.

qa.q: How long did Indu suggest for choosing the topic?
qa.a: Indu suggested five minutes.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling before making the suggestion?
qa.a: Indu was probably impatient and worried about wasted time, since the group had been going in circles since Monday.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the group use, and why?
qa.a: They could list all the ideas and vote, or let the teacher choose. Either would end the circling and let them start on the actual project.

qa.q: How might Nikhil have seen the time limit?
qa.a: Nikhil was willing to set the timer, so the limit probably felt fair and useful to Nikhil, who wanted a different topic but accepted the vote.

grounding: A girl proposes a five-minute limit with a coin toss as backup, and the limit stops the endless talk so the group can start.

subtype: Approach: one member doing everything alone [Pitfall]
passage: Class teacher's note, Wednesday. The science project group has been slow all week, and Jomon was clearly annoyed. On Tuesday night Jomon decided to finish it alone. This morning the poster arrived beautifully done, with neat writing and a working model. But Jomon's eyes were red, and Jomon yawned through the first two periods. Shreya and the other two stood at the back of the room and did not speak, and one of them said quietly that nobody had asked them. The work is good, but the group did not do it together. I will speak with each child about how to share the load.

qa.q: What did Jomon decide to do on Tuesday night?
qa.a: Jomon decided to finish the project alone.

qa.q: How might Shreya and the others be feeling at the back of the room?
qa.a: They are probably left out and hurt, since they stood silent and one said nobody had asked them.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Jomon try next time, and why?
qa.a: Jomon could tell the group what is late and ask each person to take a job with a day to finish it. That way the work is shared and nobody is tired or left out.

qa.q: How does the project look to the teacher?
qa.a: The teacher sees good work but a group that did not work together, and notices tiredness in Jomon as well as the left-out feelings.

grounding: Annoyed by delays, a member finishes the project alone at night, and the result looks good but Jomon is exhausted and the others feel left out.

subtype: Approach: asking the teacher to settle a stuck point [Revision]
passage: I'm Kamal. For two days our group had not agreed on a single plan for the model bridge. Ramesh wanted matchsticks, Tara wanted cardboard, and I wanted to stop the shouting. On Thursday I said, "We're stuck. Let's ask Miss, our teacher." We all trooped to the staff room. She listened, asked each of us for one reason, and then said, "Cardboard base, matchstick rails. And one person speaks at a time." She wrote it on a sticky note. We walked back and started measuring. Ramesh was quiet, but he handed me the ruler. That was the first time in two days that nobody argued.

qa.q: What did the teacher say the bridge would be made from?
qa.a: The bridge would have a cardboard base and matchstick rails.

qa.q: What did Kamal want when suggesting to go to the teacher?
qa.a: Kamal wanted the shouting to stop and the group to get unstuck.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the group have used earlier, and why?
qa.a: They could have listed each idea and voted, or combined the two materials themselves. A quick decision earlier would have saved the two days of arguing.

qa.q: How might Ramesh have felt about the teacher's plan?
qa.a: Ramesh was quiet but handed over the ruler, so the plan probably felt acceptable, even if Ramesh had hoped for matchsticks alone.

grounding: After two days without agreement, the group notices they are stuck and asks the teacher to settle it, and she helps them pick a plan and take turns speaking.

subtype: Approach: checking in halfway and reassigning slow tasks [Revision]
passage: Class teacher's note, Friday. Halfway through the week, Manjula stood at the front of her group and checked the chart. "Who has finished what?" Two boxes were empty: Aman's writing part. Aman had been ill on Monday and Tuesday. Manjula did not scold. "Aman, you take the labels. Jomon, can you write the first paragraph? Karan, the second." Aman looked relieved. On Friday afternoon the project was complete, and the group presented on time. I did not tell them what to do; I noticed how the group stopped, looked at the pending work and changed the plan while there was still time.

qa.q: What job did Manjula give Aman?
qa.a: Manjula gave Aman the labels.

qa.q: How might Aman have felt when the jobs were changed?
qa.a: Aman looked relieved; being ill had left the writing undone, and the easier job meant Aman did not have to catch up alone.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the group use, and why?
qa.a: They could ask the teacher to extend the deadline for the ill member. Sharing the work themselves was quicker, though, and let the project be finished on time.

qa.q: How might Jomon see being asked to write the first paragraph?
qa.a: Jomon may feel trusted with an important part, or maybe a little pressed for time, but the question was asked politely, so it was a fair request.

grounding: At the halfway check the group sees that an ill member's writing is unfinished, shares the ill member's paragraphs and gives an easier job so the project ends on time.

subtype: Approach: dividing the price by weekly pocket money [Thinking]
passage: Chinmay, come here, and I, Saurabh, will tell you how I got my first remote-control car. I was ten. It cost Rs 600 and I got Rs 50 a week. I sat with a pencil and thought aloud: 600 divided by 50 is twelve. Twelve weeks! At first that sounded forever. But then I counted twelve Sundays on the calendar, and I could see it. It was a number, not a mountain. If I skipped the ice-cream stall on some Fridays, it might even be less. So I decided: keep going, one Sunday at a time. On the twelfth Sunday I bought the car myself, and I never let it out of my sight.

qa.q: How much money did Saurabh get each week?
qa.a: Saurabh got Rs 50 a week.

qa.q: Why did Saurabh decide to keep going after working out twelve weeks?
qa.a: Saurabh saw twelve weeks as a number that could be counted and reached, and felt the goal was possible instead of impossible.

qa.q: What choice in the story could have made the wait shorter, and why?
qa.a: Skipping the ice-cream stall on some Fridays could shorten the wait, because money not spent adds to the savings each week.

qa.q: How might Chinmay see the story as the listener?
qa.a: Chinmay is being told how a big price became twelve steps, so it probably shows that a long wait can feel smaller when it is broken into weeks.

grounding: A boy divides the toy's price by weekly pocket money to get twelve weeks and decides to continue because the number seems reachable.

subtype: Approach: putting coins in a jar and marking a chart [Action]
passage: I'm Kashish. For my sketch set, I made two helpers. First, a piggy bank with a label that says 'Kashish's Art Set'. Second, a thermometer chart, drawn on the back of an old calendar, with a bulb at the bottom and a line at the top. Every Sunday I put in my coins, count them and colour one more part of the thermometer in red. On the fourth Sunday, the red had already reached the second mark. When I want to use a coin for chips, I look at the chart and change my mind. It is hard to knock down something I coloured myself.

qa.q: What does the label on the piggy bank say?
qa.a: The label says 'Kashish's Art Set'.

qa.q: Why does the chart help Kashish leave the coins alone?
qa.a: Seeing the colour rise makes Kashish feel proud and motivated, so spending on chips feels like undoing the progress.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Kashish use if progress feels slow, and why?
qa.a: Kashish could earn extra by helping at home, or set a smaller first goal to celebrate. Both would keep the effort feeling worthwhile.

qa.q: How might someone else at home see Kashish's chart?
qa.a: Someone else at home would see steady effort and a clear goal, and might be happy to help or to leave the piggy bank alone.

grounding: A girl keeps a labelled piggy bank and colours a thermometer chart each week, so seeing the colour rise keeps the coins untouched.

subtype: Approach: spending on snacks and forgetting the goal [Pitfall]
passage:
Week one, Monday. Avni got money from Papa and put half in the jar. On the way home, Avni bought chips and a packet of stickers with the rest. It was only a little, Avni told herself.

Week three, Thursday. The jar felt light. Avni shook it and counted eight coins. There had been chips on Tuesday, a sticker book on Friday, and a lollipop today. Nobody had counted any of it.

Week five, Saturday. Avni opened the jar and found almost nothing. The toy in the shop window was as far away as on the first day.

qa.q: What did Avni buy on the way home in the first week?
qa.a: Avni bought chips and a packet of stickers.

qa.q: What might Avni be feeling when opening the jar in week five?
qa.a: Avni is probably disappointed and surprised, since the jar is almost empty and the toy still feels far away. 😔

qa.q: What alternative approach could Avni use, and why?
qa.a: Avni could write down each spend and set aside the savings first, before buying snacks. Counting small spends shows where the money goes.

qa.q: How might Papa see the empty jar?
qa.a: Papa gave the money each week and would probably see how easily small spends add up, and may want to help Avni set a fixed amount aside.

grounding: A child buys chips and stickers with weekly money, and after a month the jar is nearly empty because the small spends were never counted.

subtype: Approach: earning extra by doing jobs at home [Action]
passage:
Preetam: Papa, can I earn some money? Otherwise the toy takes me twelve weeks.
Papa: Doing what?
Preetam: Washing the car every Sunday. For Rs 10.
Papa: Hmm. Bucket, soap, dry with the cloth, and no water on the seats.
Preetam: Deal!
Sabina: Wait, Preetam, if you earn Rs 10 extra, that's eight weeks instead of twelve.
Preetam: Really, Didi?
Sabina: I did the sums on the fridge board. Eight.
Preetam: Then I start this Sunday. Mummy, where's the big bucket?
Mummy: Under the sink. Don't forget the tyres.

qa.q: How much does Papa pay for washing the car?
qa.a: Papa pays Rs 10 for washing the car.

qa.q: What does Preetam want when asking Papa about earning money?
qa.a: Preetam wants to shorten the wait for the toy by earning extra, and is eager, as seen in starting this Sunday.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Preetam use as well, and why?
qa.a: Preetam could set a smaller first target or ask relatives for money at a festival. Either could shorten the wait while the Sunday job keeps adding up.

qa.q: How does Sabina see Preetam's plan?
qa.a: Sabina did the sums on the fridge board and is happy to share the result, which shows an older sister who wants the plan to work.

grounding: Preetam asks the parents whether washing the car on Sundays can earn extra money, which shortens the wait from twelve weeks to eight.

subtype: Approach: comparing shops and cheaper choices [Thinking]
passage: Rehana and her cousin Nazia stood outside the toy shop near the bus stand. The building set she wanted was on the shelf at Rs 700. "Try the market lane," said Nazia. In the market lane, the same box cost Rs 600, and the shopkeeper showed her a smaller set for Rs 450. Rehana held both boxes for a long moment. "If I take the smaller one, I can buy it in six weeks. The big one is eight weeks. But it has forty extra pieces." Nazia tilted her head. "Would you use the extra pieces?" Rehana thought about her shelf at home. Then she said, "Let me count my savings again first."

qa.q: How much did the big set cost in the market lane?
qa.a: The big set cost Rs 600 in the market lane.

qa.q: What is Rehana trying to decide, and what does Rehana seem to feel while holding both boxes?
qa.a: Rehana is weighing whether the extra pieces are worth waiting two more weeks, and seems unsure and careful. 🤔

qa.q: What alternative approach could Rehana use to decide, and why?
qa.a: Rehana could ask a friend who owns the set whether the extra pieces get used, since real experience is better than guessing. She could also save a little first and decide later.

qa.q: How does Nazia help in the choice?
qa.a: Nazia points to the cheaper shop and then asks whether Rehana would use the extra pieces, so Nazia helps her think without telling her what to do.

grounding: A girl finds the same toy cheaper at another shop and a smaller set cheaper still, and weighs whether the extra pieces are worth the wait.
